description:
The first line of the most beloved book about sisters isn't about love — it's about money: "Christmas won't be Christmas without any presents."

We've spent 150 years treating Little Women like a cozy holiday sweater. But read the ledger underneath and it's a quiet war — between the sanitized moral guide Louisa May Alcott was paid to write, and the book she couldn't help writing: a portrait of a woman who wants work, money, and freedom more than a husband. Jo March is literature's first modern career woman, smuggled inside a Christmas story.

This is a full summary and analysis of Little Women through one lens — the economics of goodness: the literal price tag on being a "good" woman in the 1860s. Jo selling her hair for $25, Amy's ruthless lime economy, Beth as the ideal Alcott had to kill, the refusal of Laurie, Professor Bhaer talking Jo out of her most profitable writing, and the marriage ending Alcott wrote almost out of spite. No fluff, no filler.
